clue.text: For example, one group of cops coming in about serious crime

indicators.note: the run of pieces comes in, entering the word for about and splitting it

parts.note: re is Latin-derived crossword shorthand for about or concerning
eg is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example
the Roman numeral for one
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the plain-clothes detectives of a British police force

explanation.surface: Police officers arrive to investigate a grave offence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming in' makes the cops' pieces enter the two letters for 'about', splitting them. CID is British police shorthand worth knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Killing a monarch is an especially grave offence, historically treated as treason of the highest order.

clue.text: Carpet material black beetle gets under

indicators.note: in a down clue the beetle gets under, placed below, the material

parts.note: rep is a ribbed fabric used in upholstery
roach is short for cockroach, often called a black beetle

explanation.surface: A black beetle crawls beneath the carpet fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' looks like a floor covering, but here it is the verb meaning to scold.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is British idiom for calling them in to rebuke them, as with a boss's carpet.

clue.text: Allow the old lady a little time?

parts.note: gran is an affectionate word for grandmother
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Give grandma a few minutes?
explanation.definitionFit: To grant is to permit or concede something, a synonym of allow.

clue.text: Who carried the can, losing head sadly?

definitions.text: Who carried the can, losing head sadly?

indicators.note: sadly signals the letters are rearranged, the misfortune shaking them up
the word can loses its head, its first letter, before the shuffle

explanation.surface: Whoever took the blame paid with their head.
explanation.walkthrough: CAN loses its first letter to leave AN; WHO, CARRIED, THE and AN are then rearranged. Henry VIII's fifth wife was beheaded in 1542.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifth wife of Henry VIII took the blame for adultery and was executed by beheading.

clue.text: The old man gets to cuddle a heavenly body, the despicable fellow!

indicators.note: to cuddle is to hold in your arms, so the father's word wraps round the rest

parts.note: old man is informal for father, dad
a star is a heavenly body

explanation.surface: Father hugs a celebrity, the scoundrel!
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets to cuddle' wraps the father round the rest. 'Dastard' is an archaic word, the root of dastardly.
explanation.definitionFit: A dastard is an old word for a contemptible, cowardly villain.

clue.text: Perplex two females beset by woe

indicators.note: the females are surrounded on all sides by the word for woe, so it wraps them

parts.note: bale is an archaic and poetic word for misery or sorrow
F is the abbreviation for female, so two of them give FF

explanation.surface: A pair of women are confused while beset by sorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beset by' wraps the woe word round the females. 'Bale' for woe survives today mainly in the adjective baleful.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to puzzle someone completely, leaving them bewildered.

clue.text: Like a blank page, ghastly to look at?

definitions.meaning: an unwritten sheet of paper is pure white
a person who looks ghastly has a deathly pale face

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is literal: an empty sheet of paper is white; the second is the idiom for pallor from shock.
explanation.definitionFit: A simile for extreme paleness, used of a frightened or ill person's face.

clue.text: Primarily fiction — but with a strange reality?

definitions.text: Primarily fiction — but with a strange reality?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, pointing to the opening letter of fiction
strange signals that the following letters are rearranged into something odd

explanation.surface: A make-believe tale nonetheless has a curious truth to it.
explanation.walkthrough: F from 'fiction' is followed by a rearrangement of A REALITY.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's story of magic and enchantment, fiction with its own strange logic.

clue.text: Overwhelm mischief-maker carrying gun around

indicators.note: the mischief-maker carries the shuffled weapon inside

parts.note: an elf is a mischievous sprite

indicators.note: around means the letters of gun are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A troublemaker armed with a gun takes over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' rearranges the gun's letters (to NGU) and 'carrying' puts them inside the elf. Elves are the classic mischievous sprites of folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: To engulf is to sweep over and swamp completely, to overwhelm.

clue.text: Member may be surrounded by this band

parts.note: an arm is a member, a limb
let means may, as in being allowed

explanation.surface: A limb might be encircled by this strip of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: an arm, a member, is encircled by this band. Only 'band' is the strict definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An armlet is a band worn round the upper arm.

clue.text: The twentieth scheme for factory?

parts.note: a scheme is a plan
T is the twentieth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A twentieth-century plan for an industrial site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The twentieth' sounds like a century but means the twentieth letter, T.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant is an industrial works or manufacturing facility, a synonym of factory.

clue.text: Bound, with something boring introduced, to be slumping untidily

indicators.note: the boring tool is introduced into the word for bound, going inside it

parts.note: to bound is to leap or spring
an awl is a pointed tool for boring holes

explanation.surface: Leaping about, then slumping in a heap after a dull interlude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something boring' suggests a dull thing; it is a tool that bores holes, and 'introduced' sets it inside the leap.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying with limbs spread out awkwardly and carelessly is what sprawling describes.

clue.text: Alert umpire may look for suspicious scratches here

definitions.meaning: alert means quick-witted and attentive, sharp

definitions.text: umpire may look for suspicious scratches here
definitions.meaning: in cricket, ball tampering means scratching the ball's surface to make it swing, so an umpire inspects the ball itself

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is literal: the scratches would be found on the cricket ball, so the umpire looks on it.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for being sharp and quick to react, as a player watching the ball closely is.

clue.text: Sick over many hours — not a very happy scene

indicators.note: the word for sick goes over, covering, the shortened hours so they sit within it

parts.note: ill means sick

indicators.note: not tells us the following a is left out of the hours

parts.note: a day is many hours, twenty-four of them

explanation.surface: Feeling ill for hours on end is hardly a blissful picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a' removes A from the day (leaving DY), and 'over' sets the sick word over it. 'not a very happy scene' reads as a sad one, but 'not a' is the deletion.
explanation.definitionFit: An idyll is a picture of perfect, peaceful contentment, often pastoral.

clue.text: Sugared drug Frank has swallowed

indicators.note: the frank word takes the drug inside it as if it were swallowing a pill

parts.note: frank means candid, open and honest
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone called Frank has taken a sweetened pill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name; it means CANDID, which takes E inside as CANDI-E-D.
explanation.definitionFit: Candied fruit is preserved by coating or soaking it in sugar.

clue.text: Number endlessly threatening someone Check tod who makes proposal

clue.text: Contemptible person captured on return — about time!

indicators.note: the reversed word for captured goes about, surrounding, the word for time
on return means the word for captured is read backwards

parts.note: got means captured, caught
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A villain is taken back into custody, and not before time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on return' turns the capture word into TOG, and 'about' wraps it round the time. TOERAG is British slang for a worthless person.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a scoundrel or despicable lowlife, the sort of rogue a policeman might collar.

clue.text: In a particular phase belt up and minute, become inactive

annotationWithheld.clue: In a particular phase belt up and minute, become inactive

clue.text: Local tourists encountered in German town

indicators.note: the word for encountered sits in the German town's name

parts.note: Ems (Bad Ems) is a spa town in Germany
met means encountered

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers bumped into each other in a German spa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places the meeting word inside the spa town. EMMETS is Cornish dialect, literally ants, for tourists swarming in each summer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cornwall the dialect word for ants is applied, not kindly, to summer visitors.

clue.text: Man with large vehicle coming up? Give way

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means both pieces together are read from bottom to top

parts.note: Tim is a man's name
a bus is a large vehicle

explanation.surface: A fellow in a big lorry approaches; better let him pass.
explanation.walkthrough: TIM then BUS, read upwards as a whole, gives SUB MIT.
explanation.definitionFit: To submit is to yield or surrender, to give way.

clue.text: End of meal? Leave after eating seconds

indicators.note: the word for leave eats the abbreviation, taking it inside

parts.note: to desert is to leave or abandon

explanation.surface: Someone walks out of dinner after a second helping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seconds' looks like a second helping but is just S; it goes inside DESERT to give DES-S-ERT.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet course comes at the close of a meal, hence the question mark on a descriptive definition.

clue.text: Go into complicated dance figure

indicators.note: into means the word go is put inside the rearranged dance
complicated signals the letters of dance are tangled into another order

explanation.surface: Get into an intricate dance step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complicated' turns the dance into DECAN and 'into' sets GO inside it. 'figure' sounds like a dance figure; it is a shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A decagon is a geometric figure with ten sides.

clue.text: A combination of notes heard in harmony

indicators.note: heard tells us to listen to the phrase spoken, not read it

parts.note: a chord is a combination of notes played together

explanation.surface: A blend of musical notes sounds harmonious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A chord' said out loud sounds like the answer; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in accord is to be in agreement, in harmony.

clue.text: Peculiar language associated with love in some poetry

parts.note: cant is the jargon peculiar to a particular group
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: Odd turns of phrase about romance in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A canto is one of the major divisions of a long poem, so it is a portion of poetry.

clue.text: Supports archbishop's well-turned speech

parts.note: backs means supports
Cosmo Lang was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1928 to 1942

explanation.surface: Endorses a churchman's eloquent address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well-turned' seems to praise the speech; it means its words are turned round, as in back slang (yob for boy).
explanation.definitionFit: Back slang is speech in which words are spoken backwards, so it is turned in a literal sense.

clue.text: What can affect muscles? A cold can

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Can a chill from a tin affect your muscles?
explanation.walkthrough: Actin is a protein in muscle fibres, working with myosin to make them contract.
explanation.definitionFit: A protein that, with myosin, drives muscle contraction, so it acts on muscles.

clue.text: Banning unruly lout wanting to join a side

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly, so the letters of lout are thrown into a new order

parts.note: a wing is a side, as of a building or a team

explanation.surface: A rowdy yob is barred from joining a team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unruly' rearranges LOUT into OUTL; 'wanting to join' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To outlaw something is to prohibit or forbid it.

clue.text: More pulling out half way through

indicators.note: we stop half way through the word for pulling out, keeping only its first half

parts.note: extracting means pulling out

explanation.surface: Someone withdraws from a task midway.
explanation.walkthrough: EXTRACTING has ten letters; its first five give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, so it is a synonym of more.

clue.text: Poke fun at some of the dire dancers falling over

indicators.note: falling over means the run of letters is read backwards
the answer is formed from some of the letters of the dancers' phrase

explanation.surface: Mocking the awful dancers as they tumble.
explanation.walkthrough: EDIRED runs through 'thE DIRE Dancers'; read backwards it gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To deride is to mock or ridicule, to poke fun at.

clue.text: Batting posture at the crease for example

parts.note: a batsman in cricket who is batting is said to be in
a batsman's stance is how they stand at the crease ready to receive the ball

explanation.surface: A batsman's position at the wicket, as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: The crease is the line where a cricket batsman stands; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case or illustration, so an example.
